framing_issues.text: The law sets aside no money and doesn't require families to pay for anything.
framing_issues.issue: Missing context and uneven caveats. In the reader-first section (lines 15-16) 'sets aside no money' appears without the budget caveat given at lines 119 and 200, and 'doesn't require families to pay for anything' reads as a promise of no cost, while line 29 says the cost to families is not known. A parent or staff member could come away more certain than the sources allow.

framing_issues.text: ### Who decides, and how to reach them
framing_issues.issue: The heading promises a way to reach decision-makers, but every entry (lines 44-46) says our sources have no contact details, so the section isn't actionable. Either archive official contact pages (General Assembly, governor, a district directory) as passages and cite them, or retitle the section 'Who decides'.

framing_issues.text: If you care most about sparing teachers from confrontations over phones / learning without distractions
framing_issues.issue: Uneven values guide. Option B gets a broad value (learning without distractions). Option A rests on one narrow quote about 'older teachers' and confrontation. The concerns opposing parents cited most, reaching a child in an emergency (74.8%, P-035; Adams, P-049) and parental choice (45.5%), get no line. Neither line names the option it points to (A or B), so readers must work it out from 'opposed the bill' or 'called for the ban'.

framing_issues.text: By Jan 1 each year ... to cover kindergarten through 12th grade. ... The first such deadline under the new law is Jan 1, 2027.
framing_issues.issue: Unexplained tension for readers: policies that must 'prohibit bell-to-bell access' through grade 12 are due Jan 1, 2027 (P-008), yet high schools may start the ban as late as July 1, 2027 (P-007; lines 22, 27, 52). A reader may think the ban starts in January. One sentence on how the two dates fit, or saying the law doesn't spell this out, would help.

framing_issues.text: you can't use phones or similar devices at any point in the school day
framing_issues.issue: 'Use' understates the rule: the law bars 'access', defined as viewing, holding, wearing or otherwise using a device (P-003). A student could read this line (also shown alone on the home page) as allowing a phone in hand or a smartwatch worn, as long as it isn't used.

framing_issues.text: A 2025 law already bars these students from using phones and similar devices during the school day.
framing_issues.issue: This first sentence is shown alone on the home page. 'These students' needs the bold label to make sense, and the sentence doesn't say that HB 1009 leaves the K-8 rule in place (that is in the next sentence). Suggest naming the grades and adding 'HB 1009 doesn't change this.'

framing_issues.text: The amendment also rewrote what "bell-to-bell" means
framing_issues.issue: Unexplained term: 'bell-to-bell' first appears here, but the page never says it is the law's name for the school-day period (P-002, P-005). Line 76 describes the period without naming it.

framing_issues.text: The quoted passage gives no measurements behind those reports.
framing_issues.issue: Internal jargon: 'the quoted passage' (also line 191) refers to the project's archived passages, which a reader can't see. Use 'The news report gives no measurements...'.

framing_issues.text: In that study, the rise in suspensions began to fade after the first year.
framing_issues.issue: Vague reference: the last study named was two bullets up (under 'What supports it'), and the bullet just before is about Woods and Harrell. Say 'In the Florida study'.

framing_issues.text: Who disagrees: The English study's authors said there is "no evidence..."
framing_issues.issue: Labels researchers as a side: the English authors reported findings about English schools and didn't comment on Georgia's law. Putting them under 'Who disagrees', next to the advocates and officials listed there on other cards, makes them look like opponents. Consider listing them under 'What challenges it' only.

framing_issues.text: In a 2025 survey of 1,002 Georgia parents ..., 70.8% supported a high school ban.
framing_issues.issue: A popularity figure listed under 'Who benefits' reads as an argument from popularity; support isn't a benefit. The reasons that follow (P-034) fit the field. Option A's 'Who benefits' has no matching figure.
